articles.title: Skid Row forgeries, illegal votes and a mayoral candidate: Election fraud cases pile up nationwide
articles.summary: Noncitizen voting and fraudulent voter registration cases were announced across several states this week, adding to DOJ's growing election fraud prosecutions from recent weeks.
articles.body: The Trump administration continues to crack down on voter fraud cases, including a noncitizen who allegedly voted in a mayoral race he was fraudulently registered for and a noncitizen arrested for allegedly lying about her citizenship to vote in federal elections. These allegations span a slate of federal election-related cases highlighted by the Justice Department in recent days, adding to a series of prosecutions targeting noncitizen voting, fraudulent voter registrations and other alleged election-related crimes. The DOJ's latest announcements involve California, Kansas, Louisiana, Texas and Massachusetts, while federal prosecutors have brought a number of other cases across the country in recent weeks amid the Trump administration's broader efforts to bolster election security ahead of the midterms. The White House pointed to the new cases that continue to pile up as evidence supporting the administration's crackdown. DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED "Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of noncitizens registering and voting in our elections continues to pile up," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "Any noncitizens found registering and voting in our elections will be arrested and held accountable. Only Americans should be electing American leaders." The more than a dozen defendants charged in cases announced this week face allegations ranging from illegal voting and false claims of U.S. citizenship to fraudulent voter registration and identity fraud. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche warned that individuals "gaming the election system, voting illegally or committing voter fraud" will face prosecution, while federal prosecutors in Texas said their seven cases "send a clear message" that laws barring noncitizens from voting will be enforced. Among the defendants were Louisiana mayoral candidate Bridget Johnson, who prosecutors allege fraudulently registered Jamaican noncitizen Michael Wedderburn before he voted in the 2024 federal election and the same mayoral race in which Johnson was a candidate. Johnson allegedly electronically submitted a Louisiana voter registration application in Wedderburn's name on July 14, 2024, falsely stating that he was a U.S. citizen, according to court documents. ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT LEARNS FATE AFTER USING STOLEN IDENTITY TO VOTE IN US ELECTIONS FOR DECADES Johnson was charged with fraudulent voter registration and voting by an alien, while Wedderburn was charged with voting by an alien. If convicted, Johnson faces up to five years in prison, while Wedderburn faces up to one year, along with potential financial penalties, according to federal prosecutors. Other cases announced this week included allegations against three people in California accused in an alleged scheme that used stolen identities of registered voters to manufacture signatures on ballot initiative petitions. California frequently uses ballot initiatives to put major policy questions directly before voters, with citizen-backed measures capable of changing state law or amending the state constitution. Recent initiatives have included Proposition 36, which increased penalties for certain drug and theft crimes, and measures dealing with the minimum wage and rent control. Prosecutors allege James Brass and Courtney Price went to Los Angeles' Skid Row, where they handed people stolen identities belonging to registered California voters and paid them to copy those voters' personal information onto ballot petitions and forge their signatures. Brass and a third defendant, Jateisha Herron, then allegedly falsely certified that they had personally witnessed the registered voters sign the petitions. Brass allegedly received about $41,600 from coordinators working with a petition-management company helping collect signatures, according to prosecutors. EX-NEW JERSEY MAYOR, HER HUSBAND CHARGED FOR USING FAKE BALLOT SIGNATURES AFTER SHE PLEADED GUILTY TO DUI The case is the second election-related federal prosecution announced this year involving alleged payments to people on Skid Row. In May, federal prosecutors charged a longtime ballot initiative signature collector with paying individuals, including homeless people living on Skid Row, to register to vote. In Kansas, prosecutors charged 24-year-old Peruvian national and U.S. permanent resident Mariana Alexandra Dewey with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship, fraudulent election conduct and voting as an alien in a federal election after arresting her earlier this month. In Massachusetts, federal prosecutors announced a case this week against Nigerian national Gladys Adaeze Okafor, who allegedly claimed to be a U.S. citizen while registering to vote before casting ballots in multiple federal elections. A handful of cases were announced by federal prosecutors in Texas this week as well, including multiple cases where individuals registered to vote illegally when applying for a Texas driver's license. On the same day those defendants were indicted, a Mexican national was also sentenced to 36 months in federal prison for aggravated identity theft, false statements of citizenship, and illegal voting by an alien, according to federal officials. INSIDE HOUSE REPUBLICANS' PLAN TO END RUN DEM OPPOSITION AND PASS TRUMP-BACKED VOTER ID The cases add to the growing list of federal election-related cases brought in the past few weeks on top of other prosecutions earlier this year involving noncitizens accused of illegally registering or voting in U.S. elections. Less than two weeks ago, the Justice Department charged five people in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Wisconsin in cases involving alleged illegal voting or fraudulent registration tied to the 2022 or 2024 elections. The DOJ separately charged an Indian national in Minnesota last week with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship in order to vote in the 2024 general election. Despite the mounting prosecutions, the Trump administration also faced a setback this week in its efforts to boost election security. The Supreme Court ruled Monday that the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) could not implement the president's stricter mail ballot requirements for the 2026 elections, leaving a lower court's nationwide injunction in place. The blocked rules would have required states to use specially designed mail ballot envelopes with unique voter barcodes, submit envelope designs to USPS for review and provide it with information about intended ballot recipients. The ruling, however, did not block a separate part of Trump's March executive order directing the federal government to create citizenship lists for states to use in checking their voter rolls. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was appointed by Trump, agreed the rules should not take effect for this year's elections, writing that state and local officials did not have sufficient time to reasonably implement them. Nonetheless, Kavanaugh said there was "at least a fair prospect" that the Postal Service ultimately has the statutory authority to impose the requirements. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented. Trump blasted the decision Tuesday as another "bad decision" from the Supreme Court and praised Alito and Thomas as "legends," while arguing the ruling would make cheating through mail ballots easier.

articles.title: Lawmakers say they are standing at the gates against 'Trojan horses' promoting malign foreign interests
articles.summary: House Foreign Affairs Committee members allege CodePink and other groups serve as "Trojan horses" for foreign influence, calling for transparency and FARA disclosure.
articles.body: WASHINGTON, D.C. — In a series of exclusive interviews with Fox News Digital, lawmakers on the House Foreign Affairs Committee sounded the alarm on a sprawling network of "Trojan horse" activists, nonprofits and social media influencers allegedly amplifying the hostile messages of foreign adversaries straight through the open gates of American democracy. The warning came into sharp focus Tuesday when CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin and two fellow activists walked into House Rayburn 2172 for a hearing on covert foreign influence operations, then strategically positioned themselves behind witnesses in T-shirts supporting the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Communist Party of Cuba. About 30 minutes into the hearing, South and Central Asia Subcommittee Chairman Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., stopped the hearing and had Capitol Police escort them out. LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION "They're coming in, trying to look like one thing, but we know that once they're inside the gates that those doors are going to spring open, and there's a whole other motivation for what they're trying to do," Huizenga told Fox News Digital. At the center of the controversy is communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, who married CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans in a tropical wedding in Jamaica in 2017, soon after funneling $285 million to six pro-China, pro-communist, anti-American nonprofits in the U.S., including CodePink, according to a Fox News Digital investigation. Lawmakers say the answer is transparency and following the money and exposing who finances the alleged "Trojan horse." In their series of interviews, Huizenga and other committee members explained how the modern "Trojan horse" isn't made of wood but rather a network of activists, nonprofits, social media influencers and other ostensibly American voices that foreign governments and foreign-linked actors can allegedly fund, amplify or exploit to carry their messages through the open gates of American democracy. "They're coming in, trying to look like one thing, but we know that once they're inside the gates that those doors are going to spring open and there's a whole other motivation for what they're trying to do," Huizenga told Fox News Digital. At the hearing, devoted to "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America," lawmakers expressed concern about how the Communist Party of China, Russia, the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Communist Party of Cuba spread their propaganda and influence in the U.S. The phrase "Trojan horse" comes from the ancient Greek story of soldiers concealed inside a wooden horse presented to the city of Troy. Once the horse was taken behind the city's fortified walls, the soldiers emerged and opened the gates, destroying Troy. Huizenga stressed that Americans can hold sincere beliefs while also having those messages funded or amplified by foreign actors without necessarily knowing it. He argued that the answer to foreign influence is exposing the origins of the messaging through transparency and robust debate. Rep. Huizenga: 'It's really about theatrics' Inside the hearing room, as Fox News Digital reported, Benjamin and her fellow CodePink activists offered a vivid illustration of the debate over how political messages are created and amplified. They sat directly behind the witnesses, placing their T-shirts in the sight line of the official committee cameras. Benjamin then turned toward a television monitor on the side of the hearing room displaying the official video feed. She pulled out her phone, zoomed in on the image of herself and a fellow activist appearing behind the witnesses and took photo after photo of the screen. HOUSE PANEL PROBES FOREIGN ‘TROJAN HORSES’ AS SINGHAM SCRUTINY WIDENS Huizenga said he viewed the episode as political theater designed for an audience beyond the committee room. "This isn't about discourse. This is about disruption," Huizenga told Fox News Digital. "It's all planned out. You see people in the crowd filming with their phones, getting ready. You knew something was going to happen because, all of a sudden, the phones would come out. "It's really about theatrics," he added, arguing that confrontations can subsequently be circulated on social media to attract attention, donations and volunteers. The episode captured the central tension running through the hearing: How does the United States expose genuine covert foreign influence without treating protected American political speech as foreign subversion? "Transparency. Transparency is the watchword," Huizenga told Fox News Digital. "We really need to make sure that people know not only the why, but the who is behind all this." Rep. Baumgartner: 'We need to know who's behind it' Rep. Michael Baumgartner, R-Wash., told Fox News Digital that America's open political system creates opportunities for foreign governments to try to influence legitimate domestic debates through social media, universities and other institutions. "The American people need transparency and need to understand what is going on in these public policy discussions and whether it's podcast hosts, certain actors on social media or things going on our college campuses," Baumgartner said. "We need to know who's behind it and what their motivations are." Baumgartner pointed to "clear transparency on this issue" as a solution, adding that if evidence showed organizations were acting on behalf of foreign governments without complying with applicable disclosure laws, the matter could potentially be referred to the Justice Department, which oversees the Foreign Agent Registration Act, or FARA. The law requires that people and organizations acting on behalf of foreign interests register with the Justice Department. Rep. Randy Fine: Trojan horses ‘poison people’s minds’ Other lawmakers said the modern Trojan horse doesn't necessarily have to walk physically through the doors of Congress, but rather arrive via social media. Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., described social media, influencers and protests as potential channels through which foreign governments influence American political debate. He said "it's a real issue, whether it's on social media, influencers, protests, these things are all designed to destabilize our country." Fine characterized what experts call "cognitive warfare" as "using our information platforms to try to poison people's minds and to create division from within." Rep. Darrell Issa: ‘It’s a network’ Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., focused on another battlefield: artificial intelligence. "Trojan horses are things like the announcement that we should slow down on AI," Issa told Fox News Digital, arguing that foreign adversaries can benefit when American political pressure slows U.S. technological development. "We are in a war in which the other side uses all the clandestine tools," Issa said. "They use their, quite frankly, their social media to our detriment." Huizenga similarly argued that Americans should view the organizations under examination not individually but as a network. "It's a network. It's not independent organizations or even people," he said. "You will see some of the same people at different organizations, rallies, or protests." ‘Origins aren’t organic’ At the center of much of the hearing were findings from a Fox News Digital investigation into Neville Roy Singham, an American-born communist tech tycoon who lives in Shanghai and has pumped $285 million into six nonprofits, including CodePink, the People's Forum and other groups examined during the hearing. Huizenga alleged in his official opening remarks that Singham uses his wealth and relationships in China to support organizations that promote communist ideology and destabilize American society. He explicitly described Singham, CodePink and a growing network of pro-communist, pro-China groups as "Trojan horses." ‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA Singham and CodePink have denied taking direction from the Chinese government. Singham has said his activities reflect his own political beliefs, while Benjamin has said CodePink doesn't receive money from the Chinese Communist Party. As Fox News Digital reported in June, the Justice Department and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York have convened a grand jury investigation into alleged money laundering, bank fraud and wire fraud by Singham and the organizations he has funded. No criminal charges have been filed against Singham or CodePink with respect to those allegations. Huizenga argued that the funding relationships deserve scrutiny. "Oftentimes, it's frankly the origins aren't organic, or if there is a part of it being organic, this is getting fed by outside organizations, oftentimes even outside countries," Huizenga alleged. ‘Transparency is the watchword’ Being escorted through the committee room doors didn't end CodePink's political theater. Outside the hearing room, Benjamin positioned herself beside the House Foreign Affairs Committee placard and began recording another video, pulling out a comb first to straighten her hair. When Rep. Fine emerged from the hearing, Benjamin followed him down the hallway firing questions as another member of her team recorded the encounter. After Fine disappeared into an office, Benjamin returned to the committee entrance, straightened her hair with a comb and resumed recording. HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS About two hours after Capitol Police escorted the activists from the hearing, CodePink posted a carefully edited video of the day's confrontation on social media, where activists in the broader network began sharing it. The physical protest was over, but the images it produced were just beginning to travel. That sequence was precisely why lawmakers said Americans should look beyond the spectacle to who finances and amplifies political messaging. "This is theater for many of these people," Huizenga said. He said he wanted Americans, through "transparency and disclosure," to understand "not just the what they are doing, but the who is financing them." The lawmakers gathered to investigate modern "Trojan horses" said the lesson of the ancient story wasn't simply to keep the horse outside the gates but also to understand what — and who — might be inside. "Transparency. Transparency is the watchword," Huizenga said. Lawmakers say 'transparency and disclosure' are the best defense against influence campaigns exploiting America's democracy. articles.title: Top Democrat Gregory Meeks opposes US sale of heavy bombs to Israel
articles.summary: But the objection is not enough to stop the sale - the Trump administration can still press ahead.
articles.body:
The top Democrat on a congressional committee that reviews weapons deals has said he will not support a proposed $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale to Israel.

Gregory Meeks said he would not back the transfer of 2,000lb (900kg) bombs to Israel over concerns they might not be used in accordance with international law.

The New York congressman's objection follows reports that the US is planning to supply Israel with 40,000 of what Meeks called "some of the most destructive munitions in our arsenal".

But his objection is not enough to stop the sale - President Donald Trump's administration can sidestep Congress and press ahead anyway.

Meeks, a ranking member on the House of Representatives Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement he remained committed to Israel's security.

But he said that the deal "raises grave, unresolved concerns about how these munitions could be used in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon".

He said it reflected Congress's "responsibility to ensure that US-funded weapons are used lawfully, responsibly, and with meaningful safeguards for human life".

The BBC has asked the Israeli Embassy for comment.

J Street, a liberal pro-Israel advocacy group, said in a statement to Israeli newspaper Haaretz: "You cannot rebuild Gaza with 2,000lb bombs."

Lawmakers are informed by the US state department about arms sales exceeding a set dollar amount, allowing them to place an informal hold on the deal.

But the president can go ahead with the deal if he declares that an emergency requires an immediate sale.

A veto-proof resolution passed jointly by two-thirds of the House and Senate would be required to block the weapons transfer.

Israel's use of General Dynamics-manufactured 2,000lb bombs in Gaza has drawn international anger owing to their devastating effects in densely populated civilian areas.

In 2024, then-President Joe Biden paused a shipment of the bombs to Israel - a move reversed when President Trump returned to office last year.

The supply of the weapons is reported to be under Foreign Military Financing, a programme funded by American taxpayers that provides billions of dollars each year for Israel and other allies to buy US-made weapons.

The US-Israel relationship still has substantial bipartisan backing, but support has been softening among Democrats.

In July, Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie forced a vote on a bill to cut $3.3bn in security aid to Israel and he received support from 103 Democrats in the chamber. He was the only Republican to support the amendment.

articles.title: Dem insurgent turns on the charm with party establishment as Schumer leaves bitter feud hanging
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed met with Chuck Schumer and Senate Democrats at DSCC headquarters in Washington, D.C., but few would say if primary wounds had healed.
articles.body: Michigan’s insurgent progressive Senate nominee ran as far as he could from Washington, D.C., but on Wednesday he traveled to the nation’s Capitol for a closed-door meeting with top Democratic brass as the race for power intensifies. Abdul El-Sayed met with top Senate Democrats just hundreds of yards away from Congress, where lawmakers and the wunderkind candidate huddled to discuss his campaign and how to keep Michigan blue. Many left boasting that the Wolverine State would not turn a shade of purple. But, few, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., would say whether the fences broken during El-Sayed’s primary fight had been mended. SCHUMER DUCKS QUESTION ON CAMPAIGNING WITH SOCIALIST CANDIDATE WHO REFUSES TO BACK HIM AS LEADER "Look, we have to win Michigan and we had a great and friendly meeting," Schumer said when asked by Fox News Digital if he and El-Sayed had moved on from their differences. Still, El-Sayed held court with Democratic brass for hours at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s (DSCC) headquarters in Washington, where a steady flow of lawmakers — both allies and skeptics of his Senate bid — milled in and out of the building throughout the day. Schumer and Democrats are confident and determined that they can flip the Senate, which Republicans hold at a 53 to 47 margin. Losing Michigan to the GOP and former Rep. Mike Rogers would serve a mortal blow to that push. "He’s gonna win," Sen. Kirstin Gillibrand, D-N.Y., who is also the DSCC chair, said. The key mission for Democrats is getting independents and Republicans on the fence. But few, including Schumer, said that they would actually hit the campaign trail with El-Sayed. It all comes after El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., locked horns in one of the most bitter Democratic primary fights of this cycle that pitted the Democratic old-guard versus a progressive movement gaining steam across the country. SEE IT: DEM SENATORS RALLY BEHIND EL-SAYED BUT DUCK QUESTIONS ON PROGRESSIVE AGENDA Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., who initially endorsed Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow before she dropped out, told Fox News Digital that, "obviously, primaries can get really hot, and the Michigan primary got hot." "This is what you do after a primary is you try to unite the party and then you do the work to reach out and cross over to independent voters and Republican voters," Murphy said. "So I don't think anybody should be surprised that he's trying to build bridges after a heated primary. That's what good candidates, that's what winning candidates do." Another McMorrow backer, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., painted a rosy picture of the closed-door session, and noted that it was "hard to hear in there because so many people were talking and laughing and wanted to hear about the campaign." "He makes good connections because it's a lot of people in there who are talking about what can we do next? What can we do to lower costs for families? What can we do to make this government work better for working people? So it was a very enthusiastic, very cheerful group of people," she said. Retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., whose seat El-Sayed is gunning for, initially endorsed Stevens. Now, he’s shifting gears. DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE "I'm endorsing him, and he's been getting support across the board in Michigan. The Democrats are coming together," Peters said in response to a question about whether the Democratic establishment was uniting behind El-Sayed. "We understand how important this election is." Others were more keen to lend an assist to El-Sayed, including Murphy and Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., who said, "I’m gonna be in Michigan here in a couple of weeks." Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., who is running for re-election in deep blue Massachusetts, said that Democrats’ strategy heading into the final stretch was pitching an affordability agenda, and that El-Sayed "is the answer." "I'm helping him. I think we're all gonna help," Markey said when asked if he would fundraise with El-Sayed. The specter of El-Sayed’s relationship with controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who helped to amplify his campaign in the primary battle, wasn’t something that Democrats focused on during their huddle. "Hasan what?," Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-N.Y., told Fox News Digital when asked if he came up during the meeting. "I don’t even know who that is." When asked if Piker came up, or if Democrats encouraged El-Sayed to further distance himself from him, Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, "Not in terms of the conversation. Like I said, I was just trying to get to know him." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP After initially dodging Fox News Digital’s question on whether he would campaign with Piker, El-Sayed later told reporters that, "This conversation is so far removed from what people are talking about." "Everyday, in Michigan, people sit at their kitchen tables and ask ‘how am I going to make this work next month?’ That’s not a middle, right, left issue, that’s a basic affordability issue," El-Sayed said. But when further pressed, he countered that Michigan voters "really don’t care about that." "They really don't," El-Sayed said.
